To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

we have presented a detailed dynamic finite-strain computational model of the left ventricle of the human heart that is derived from clinical imaging of a healthy subject and also from a patient with MI.
we developed dynamic computational models of human LV mechanics in health and disease and showed that the models can accurately reproduce subject-specific CMR strain measurements.

we have developed a novel, dynamic, subject-specific finite-strain model of the human LV based on CMR-derived geometry and material parameters, and that the model is capable of simulating the LV dynamics of both a healthy human subject and a patient with an MI.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of subject-specific dynamic models of human LV mechanics.
the development of a new computational framework for the dynamic simulation of the human LV in health and disease.
the development of subject-specific dynamic models of the human LV that are derived from CMR imaging data.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the IBFEM models of the human LV presented in this work can be used to predict the detailed dynamics of the human LV, including the three-dimensional distributions of deformation, stress, strain and strain rate in the ventricular wall, from a knowledge of the subject-specific geometry and the material properties of the ventricular wall.
our models are in good agreement with experimental observations.

the IB-FEM model is a promising tool for modelling the heart, and that this tool can be used to provide detailed information about the mechanics of the human heart that cannot be obtained from conventional clinical measurements.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we have developed a detailed computational model of the human left-ventricle that can accurately simulate its dynamic behaviour from end-diastole to end systole.

the dynamic finite-strain models of the heart that have been developed in this work are capable of simulating realistic LV kinematics in health and in disease and can be used to study the biomechanical effects of disease on the LV.
the present models can be employed to predict detailed three-dimensional strain and stress fields within the human LV in health and disease.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the combination of detailed structural mechanics and constitutive modelling with the IB method is a powerful tool for modelling the biomechanics and function of the human heart.

it is possible to build detailed computational models of the LV that are based on clinical CMR images, and that these models can be used for patient-specific simulations of the LV dynamics and for patient-specific risk stratification.

dynamic models of the human LV can be constructed from CMR imaging data, that these models can be used to estimate detailed stress distributions, and that these models are capable of reproducing a range of experimental data.
